business_problem: Bayernwerk's transformer-station commissioning process relied on paper forms, manual image uploads, and back-office re-entry into SAP, creating weeks-long delays, human error, and difficulty keeping computer-vision models reliable as hardware variants and user volume grew.
solution_summary: Bayernwerk digitized transformer-station commissioning with NEXT.SwitchON, a tablet application that captures field data and photos during onsite work. The app uses machine-learning computer vision to identify installed hardware and wiring from tablet images and pre-fill digital documentation. The resulting records are transferred into Bayernwerk's end system, SAP, instead of being re-entered from paper. To make the AI reliable in production, Bayernwerk ran the solution on Socrates, an Azure-based integration platform implemented by DXC, and added DXC MLOps Quickstart for Microsoft Azure. DXC then converted the initial ML approach into scalable, reusable pipelines that automate image augmentation, model training, evaluation, CI/CD-based deployment, continuous monitoring, event-driven retraining, model orchestration, and publishing the newest models back into NEXT.SwitchON.
products_used: DXC MLOps Quickstart for Microsoft Azure

data_flow: Technicians use NEXT.SwitchON on tablets to capture installation data and take photos of transformer-station work. Computer vision models identify hardware and wiring from the images and pre-fill digital documentation. Through the Socrates platform on Azure, the records are transferred into SAP, while the DXC MLOps Quickstart pipelines augment images, train and evaluate models, monitor them in production, and publish new model versions back to NEXT.SwitchON.
business_outcome: Bayernwerk standardized and simplified transformer-station documentation, made the computer-vision solution scalable and more reliable, reduced manual model-update work, improved image-recognition accuracy, and cut annual operating costs.
